metadata.title: Add transform offset to Control nodes

issue_payload.body:
This is an implementation of my proposal outlined in this discussion: https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/7053#issuecomment-1883816733

**See the most recent state of this PR here: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/87081#issuecomment-3904492472**

tl;dr: Currently it's hard and complicated to animate Control nodes without breaking the layout, especially if the Control nodes are in deeply nested layout structures which is often the case. This PR adds new properties to Control nodes that specify a render transform that does not affect and is not affected by layouting (similar to CSS' `transform`). These make UI animations much less pain to work with

- `render_offset`: translation
- `render_scale`: scale
- `render_rotation`, rotation
- `render_transform_pivot`, pivot for scaling and rotating

`render_offset` and `render_transform_pivot` are relative to the size of the Control node by default (I think it's a very common usecase to rotate around and scale from the center) but it can be toggled to use absolute pixel values instead.

[Screencast from 2024-01-11 17-10-13.webm](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/assets/8849554/28f2f723-6b9f-4687-b7de-0e6c06695837)

## Considerations

~~Input is currently *not* affected by the render transform. That means if you e.g. apply a render offset to a button, the button is still clickable at its original position but drawn somewhere else. This might need some discussion whether that's desirable or not.~~ There is a toggle for this now.

discussion_timeline.author: KoBeWi
discussion_timeline.body:
I think this is the only way to reliably animate Control nodes inside Container with AnimationPlayer when their size is undetermined. Which is nice, but I think such strict requirement is not that common. There are multiple workarounds and if all fails, you can use Tweens.

That said, I think there is a way to have this feature without much overhead (currently, aside from memory, it also makes transforming more complex). The `render_*` stuff can be moved to a separate struct, which is null by default. Once any render property is set for the first time, allocate the struct. This limits the additional memory usage to single pointer for most Controls and allows to opt-out from the transform operations when the struct is null. Though not sure if doing this is a good idea 🤔

Other than that, since this is purely visual, should these properties be serialized in the scene? Especially with the input problem you mentioned? The new properties should have their purpose documented in Control's class description (i.e. that they are meant only for animation). If the usage is optional like I described above, and it's properly documented, I think it *might* be fine to have this feature.

EDIT:
Though looking at the proposal again, I think this can be a new Container too. The only argument against that was that Control workflow involves lots of nesting, but it's fine in this case, because you'd use this container only for this specific case. Also in a scene with 10 levels of nesting, one extra node is irrelevant.

EDIT2:
Then again, such container is quite easy to do in GDScript, as even noted in the proposal.

*Warning: personal opinion and experiences.* :slightly_smiling_face: 


> I think this is the only way to reliably animate Control nodes inside Container with AnimationPlayer when their size is undetermined. Which is nice, but I think such strict requirement is not that common.

I must completely disagree with your statement about this not being a common requirement. In every project so far that involves UI, a feature to apply a render transform to Control nodes of different kinds would have made things much easier to create. And it already helped a lot since I use a fork with this PR applied. Yes, I could have used Tweens for many of the things that I animated, but next to not being able to react to transform changes in parent nodes, Tweens just cannot hold up to the iteration speed and quality that AnimationPlayer gives. Being able to change animation easing curves and previewing them with one click - or even using Bezier curves - is a huge reduction in effort that I need to spend to get the same results in comparison to using Tweens. Looking at the reactions to this PR and the proposal, I don't seem to be alone with this opinion.


> That said, I think there is a way to have this feature without much overhead (currently, aside from memory, it also makes transforming more complex).

0.18% more memory usage in the most UI heavy Godot project that I know of (the Editor) still does not sound like much overhead to me, but a solution like you pointed out sounds like a good compromise, if it's really a concern.


> Also in a scene with 10 levels of nesting, one extra node is irrelevant.

I would agree immediately if Godot had some kind of slot mechanism that lets you define where children should be inserted for instanced scenes. Too often have I been at a point where I got screwed by this to be able to agree here right now. I have had dozens of such cases where this deep nesting of controls prevented modularization of logical Control "components" into separate scenes. I cannot tell immediately if this would be a problem if render transformation is achieved using Containers.

discussion_timeline.author: Mickeon
discussion_timeline.body:
TL:DR: Memory and performance overhead.
Albeit it was tested to be small for today's standards, in the most ideal scenario there should be none at all when the new render properties are not used, which is in the grand majority of cases.
The [proposed **TransformContainer**](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/98955) addresses this problem because:
- it is opt-in (you _have_ to choose where to use it), meaning there's only overhead where necessary
- using a container node is the most fitting for Godot to have this kind of feature, according to some maintainers
	- > A container does seem more like the Godot-way of doing things
	- > Wrapping containers is how SwiftUI does it 

However, as other users have brought up with their own experience, the container workflow becomes quite inconvenient and tedious for anything more complex than a few nodes. Most notably, everything that _may_ be animated in an UI needs to be wrapped inside one, which makes accessing the underlying node(s) very annoying, even in code.
See also a [small recent discussion on RocketChat](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/new-contributors?msg=StLjMYKLaxNbe9Lnt).

What was roughly suggested to address this, and I'm quoting other maintainers here [from a past discussion](https://chat.godotengine.org/channel/core?msg=vmcKidsLgtSGfWjso):
> The way to solve the memory issue is to store a pointer instead of storing the actual data
> The pattern we use in other places in the engine is to wrap the properties in a struct. Then create an instance of that struct when the object is created. The memory for the struct will be stored on its own and the only overhead in the actual object will be the pointer

> I'd be surprised if it was an inherent property in many UI frameworks. Animatable properties are usually only used temporarily, so creating a permanent performance cost for them isn't great

However, it's really worth noting that memory-wise this may also do not much:
> You would need to profile the code to find out. Memory alignment + size issues are extremely difficult to figure out in advance without profiling

I was asked to give my opinion on both proposed solutions for the problems.
From my experience making games I absolutely dislike the TransformContainers solution (The "Godot Way" is not the good way automatically) and I think this PR here is absolutely the way to go forward.

I hate the idea that animating an element requires planning and extra Node structure in place.

Making games (and animating UI) is an iterative process. Sometimes you want to animate something and the next day you decide the animation is better in some other place or not having it at all. Changing the scene everytime is beyond painful and takes a lot of the joy and ease of use out of the work that Godot excels so much at.

I don't need to use a "TransformNode3D" to animate a 3D node. I don't need a "TransformNode2D" to animate a 2D node. Why should the **underlying concept** be different for UI? It is hard to teach and complicated and annoying to use. It could break working scene scripts because of node references that suddenly change because you added an extra node just to add an animation.

**This PR here is the way to move forward.**

Just jumping in here to highlight some of the discussions that have happened between a few of us. 

From what I can tell, the goal is to allow animating the transform + pivot of control nodes to add a bit of juice (which differs from taking absolute control over the transform and ignoring the parent container). 

In Godot 3.x this was possible by animating the rotation, scale, position, or pivot directly. 

In Godot 4.0 we lost that ability. We removed access to the transform + pivot in https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/30623 since users were modifying the properties directly in editor, and then losing the modifications when the parent changed layout (due to running the scene, or modifying the parent in editor). It seems that the people involved with this change didn't realize how valuable the existing behaviour was for adding juice and ended up throwing out the baby with the bathwater. 

Now we have two competing PRs to get that behaviour back. Ironically, we can restore the 3.x behaviour with a few lines of code https://github.com/clayjohn/godot/commit/eb0d4459b5736604506acaf30acdfca412cdc1dd (this was provided to me by @BlooRabbit who has been using it in production for awhile). 

That is to say we actually have 3 competing implementations to choose between:

The big factors are:
1. Needs to support animation
2. Performance impact
3. Complexity of implementation
4. Editor UX/workflow
5. Whether input is affected

**1. Introduce a new transform node**

Pros:
- Builds on the concept of parent/child containers (argued by some to be the "Godot way" of doing things)
- Avoids complexity in Control
- Transform survives parent container changes

Cons:
- More complicated workflow (need to add a parent TransformContainer to every Node you want to animate)
- Performance, introduces several transformations on parent re-sort

This approach only impacts rendering, input does not move with the object

**2. Add render_transform properties (this PR)**

Pros:
- Simple UX, simplest workflow
- Transform survives parent container changes

Cons:
- Adds complexity to Control compared to the other approaches (but doesn't add much complexity overall)
- Performance, introduces several transformations each time you edit the transform

This approach impacts rendering, input does not move with the object

**3. animate transform directly (Godot 3.x approach)**

Pros:
- Simplest code change, no added complexity to Control
- Simple UX, simplest workflow
- Lowest performance cost

Cons:
- Affected by parent container layout changes. Modifications will be lost when parent changes

This approach impacts both input and rendering. You are actually moving the control node itself

### Summary

Based on the feedback here and on https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/98955 it is clear that this is the preferred approach between the two. I agree that this PR is preferable. 

However, I also see some outstanding disagreement on whether the input area should change in response to the animation. When comparing this PR to the 3.x approach, the biggest differences are in:
1. Whether the animated changes to transform are lost when the parent container changes
2. Whether the input rect is transformed as well

So a final question for those involved. **Which behaviour is more important? Is it more important to have the input rect move along with the rendered rect, or is it more important that the animation changes survive any changes to the parent container?**

_edit: As a final final thought. I believe that we could probably get both behaviours if we wanted to by doing something that is part way in between this PR and the Godot 3.x approach. The important thing for us to understand and agree on is how important it is for input to be affected by the animation transform_

discussion_timeline.author: AdriaandeJongh
discussion_timeline.body:
I've been thinking about what to do about the range of opinions here. Adding a slew of new properties should never be taken lightly. There appear to be two main trains of thought in the discussions here; one that pleas for new properties that stay away from the existing transform properties, and another that pleas to (re-)use the existing transform properties. They are both, after all, sets of almost identical properties.

By current thinking on the mentioned subjects is now as follows:

I think the transform offset that is proposed here **is** part of the layouting system. After all, offsetting the transform is only useful when you can't set the transform directly because the Control node you're editing is a child of a Container – because if it were not, you could _and should_ just set its transform and anchor properties directly. Following that train of thought, I subsequently think there are two approaches here:

A) We add the slew of new properties and keep all the functionality as it works today. I _would_ put the Offset Transform category inside the Layout category just like the Transform, entirely underneath the `layout/transform` as part of the Layout category, eg. `layout/offset_transform`, because I continue to believe that the functionality behind this PR is only relevant when working in a layout. As a matter of fact, I would perhaps also only show this whole section when the parent is a Container to further avoid users messing with it outside of containers.

B) We add a toggle in Layout (eg. `Enable Offset Transform`) to enable using the fields in Layout > Transform for offsetting. If disabled (by default), the transform properties show as they now do in master; as read-only. But if it is enabled, the properties inside Layout > Transform become editable. Like approach A, we should seriously consider only showing the Enable Offset Transform toggle when this control is a child of a container. One funky thing about this approach in general is that you can no longer see the read-only values like position and size, which can be relevant info when designing or debugging your UI. Regardless, I can see multiple ways of implementing approach B:

B1) We _actually_ reuse the properties of Layout > Transform to determine the offset. The only funky thing with this solution is that the proposed new properties contain one property that the current `layout/transform` category doesn't have, namely the relative position offset, which I think.... would then have to be made visible only when the offset transform toggle is enabled. A bit messy, but workable.

or

B2) The toggle swaps out the whole Transform category for the Offset Transform category by hiding the Transform category and showing the Offset Transform category. That way the properties don't _actually_ get reused; it's just that they are not visible when it's not applicable. 

Both approaches are quite close to each other. You could even argue that A and B2 are basically the same from a user perspective with the only difference being where the `Enable Offset Transform` toggle goes. Regardless, I think these are our three options when it comes to implementation.

I think I could be swayed to another approach, but I have a slight preference for approach A because it keeps the properties separate and the read-only values visible. Would love to hear other's thoughts. Maybe others here even have another approach to how this could work?

- Turbulence Mode: Control if turbulence will be used and the turbulence style.
- Turbulence Noise Contrast: Controls the contrast of the turbulence noise.
- Turbulence Noise Scale: Controls the overall scale of the turbulence noise pattern
- Turbulence Noise Speed: Controls the movement speed of the turbulence noise pattern (vec3)
- Turbulence Noise Speed Random: Randomizes the Noise Speed - this helps to break up visual patterns if they are visible.
- Turbulence Influence over life : This controls how much each particle will be influenced by the turbulence over it's lifetime
- Position Influence : How much the turbulence influences each particles position (translation)
- Velocity Influence : How much the turbulence influences each particles velocity
- Color Ramp : Offers the option to multiply each particles color with this ramp depending on the turbulence direction

![turbulence_options](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/9423774/161747519-bb753465-2f4c-499c-bbe8-534f02e56470.jpg)

metadata.title: Improvements to SplitContainer including a drag bar background StyleBox

issue_payload.body:
Improves `SplitContainer` in a number of ways making it much easier to script, and tidies up the code as follows:

- A new `split_bar_background` `StyleBox` allows solid color, gradients or textures to fill in the split bar behind or in place of the grabber icon.
- An essential new property `drag_area_scrollbar_offset` is required if one of the child controls has a scrollbar or other selectable control up against the split bar, in order to prevent the drag area from blocking mouse selection of the scroll bar or control.
- New signals `drag_started` and `drag_released` make it easier to script saving and restoring the `split_offset`
- A new property `dragging_enabled` separates dragging from `dragger_visibility` so the appearance of the drag bar is independent from whether dragging is enabled or not.
- A new method `get_drag_area_control` returns the `Control` so buttons or any other type of `Control` can ride along with the split bar (see demo video below).
- New properties `drag_area_margin_begin` and `drag_area_margin_end` allow for scripting the long-axis size of the drag area and background, which makes some nice uses like drawers simple to script (see video below).
- A new `drag_area_highlight_in_editor` property allows you to see the drag area during development.

<del>- A new virtual method `_splits_ready()` with a corresponding signal so a script knows when the split container children have been resized after the initial sort. This was a big problem because formerly, `SplitContainer._ready()` was called before the children had been fit to the container, and there was no easy way to get that information.</del>

This PR also fixes this issue and adds the theme fix: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/71862  and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/71861

Adds this enhancement https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/61534

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33969780/216680051-759ef971-ccf9-4601-a3d6-096fac0a4939.mov

This is all the GDScript neccessary for the buttons:
```
func _ready():
	var button := $Button
	var button_right := $ButtonRight
	remove_child(button)
	remove_child(button_right)
	hsplit.get_drag_area_control().add_child(button)
	hsplit.get_drag_area_control().add_child(button_right)
	button.position.y = -150 
	button_right.position.y = -50
```
https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33969780/216681485-67b85ff1-5e9f-4876-816f-30a5ecb51ba8.mov


https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33969780/216682037-9279d71b-3014-4049-a2cc-19ae316425ae.mov

Here's the editor with the drag areas visible:

https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/33969780/216685254-c85713c1-e70b-4a71-8698-8932742ba855.mov

_Production edit:_ Closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/61534, closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/6230 and closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/6231.
